Tanker struck by projectiles deep in the Persian Gulf for first time in about a month

Casualties were reported and authorities are now investigating, UK Maritime Trade Operations said, without identifying the ship or saying who was responsible.

Weilun Soon  and  Stephen Stapczynski

08 October, 2026 11:35 am IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Representational Image | Crude oil tankers, bulk carriers and vessels sit anchored around Qaboos Port on June 22, 2026 in Muscat, Oman. The Strait of Hormuz | Bloomberg

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

A tanker was struck by projectiles off the coast of Qatar on Wednesday, according to a report from UK Maritime Trade Operations, a rare attack deep inside the Persian Gulf.

The vessel was hit north of Madinat ash Shamal, at the country’s tip. Casualties were reported and authorities are now investigating, UKMTO said, without identifying the ship or saying who was responsible.

It’s the first reported strike on a tanker deep within the gulf in about a month. On Sept. 9, UKMTO said a vessel was hit by an unknown projectile about 28 nautical miles southeast of Al-Faw, Iraq. Most of the attacks since then have been concentrated in or around the Strait of Hormuz.

Show Full Article

The strike comes as the conflict between Washington and Tehran heats up once again. The White House has asked the Pentagon to draw up attack options against Iran that could be executed before the midterm elections in the US, the Atlantic reported, citing two administration officials. The size and targets of the potential strikes, and whether the administration will proceed, are still being debated, according to the report.

Iran has also increased the pace of attacks on ships in Hormuz, with UKMTO — an organization that provides a link between commercial shipping and the military — reporting nine attacks in the waterway so far this month. That’s about half of the amount reported in the whole of September, an uptick that coincides with recovering oil traffic.

The strike on Wednesday highlights the risk of more attacks extending beyond Hormuz as fighting spreads elsewhere in the Middle East. Iranian-backed Houthi rebels claimed hits on airports in Riyadh and Abha in Saudi Arabia this week that killed three people and injured dozens, as fighting intensifies between the group and Saudi-backed forces in Yemen.

CrowdStrike says China-based suspect used AI tools in South Korean bank hacks

Reuters

08 October, 2026 08:00 am IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

(c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2026

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

By Kyu-seok Shim and Brenda Goh SEOUL, Oct 8 (Reuters) – The suspect behind recent cyberattacks targeting South Korea’s financial sector may be a 26-year-old based in China’s Guangdong province who used a Chinese-developed AI agent tool called ARTEX and Anthropic’s Claude Code, US cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike said.

In a report published on Wednesday, CrowdStrike said it uncovered personal details linked to the suspected attacker while analysing AI coding-tool sessions and infrastructure associated with a campaign targeting South Korean financial institutions from late September to early October.

The case is likely to intensify concerns over the rise of AI agents and whether organisations are prepared to defend their systems against them.

Show Full Article

Australia said last month that an OpenAI autonomous agent breached a government health statistics portal in June, marking one of the first known instances of an AI agent hacking a government system.

CrowdStrike said the attacker used ARTEX, a recently released Chinese-developed open-source penetration testing tool, alongside large language models such as Claude.

“While this activity has not been attributed to a named adversary, the threat actor is likely a Chinese speaker and financially motivated,” it said.

“This assessment is made with moderate confidence based on the use of the Chinese-developed tool ARTEX and observed Chinese-language prompts.”

BANK HACKS

CrowdStrike said the individual also asked Claude where threat actors typically sell Korean data breach information and sought assistance in finding Korean Telegram data sales groups.

In another session, the person also requested Claude to create a security researcher resume, which included details such as a Telegram account, age, educational background and a location in Maoming, a city in the southern Chinese province of Guangdong, which CrowdStrike said likely belonged to the attacker.

A man who answered a phone number provided by CrowdStrike in its report said he had no knowledge of the matter.

Anthropic, South Korean police and China’s foreign ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

ARTEX is an open-source AI agent for automated penetration testing that was published on GitHub this year by a Chinese security engineer with the handle Autumn. It is not a standalone large language model but connects to external LLMs such as ChatGPT, Claude and DeepSeek to help organisations test for vulnerabilities in the networks.

The tool’s GitHub page says it is intended for personal learning, code research and local technical verification and should not be used to conduct real-world testing against online systems or websites.

At least nine South Korean banks have disclosed or have been reported by local media as having been targeted by cyberattacks since late September, prompting South Korean police to launch a probe this week and President Lee Jae Myung to call for robust response measures.

Shinhan Bank said last week that personal information of about 25,000 of its customers was compromised, while KB Kookmin Bank said that the personal information of 119 of its customers was leaked.

(Reporting by Kyu-seok Shim and Brenda Goh. Additional reporting by Maggie Grether in Seoul and Eduardo Baptista in Beijing; Editing by Chris Reese and Ed Davies)

SEOUL, Oct 8 (Reuters) – The suspect behind recent cyberattacks targeting South Korea’s financial sector may be a 26-year-old based in China’s Guangdong province, US cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike said.

In a report published on its website on Wednesday, CrowdStrike said it uncovered personal details linked to the suspected attacker while analysing AI coding-tool sessions and infrastructure associated with a campaign targeting South Korean financial institutions from late September to early October.

CrowdStrike said the attacker used ARTEX, a recently released Chinese-developed open-source penetration testing tool, alongside large language models and assessed with “moderate confidence” that the actor was a Chinese speaker and likely financially motivated.

Show Full Article

The firm said one Claude Code session contained a request to create a security researcher resume describing results from the hacking activity.

The prompt included details such as a Telegram account, age, education background and a location in Maoming, Guangdong, the report said.

CrowdStrike said the same Telegram username appeared in other cyber activity, including vulnerability research involving a Telegram-based NFT marketplace and a separate suspected attack on a Chinese payment platform.

The company said the personal details likely belonged to the actor responsible for the activity, but cautioned that currently available information could not definitively identify the attacker.

Authorities in Seoul are investigating cyberattacks that affected multiple financial institutions after banks including Shinhan Bank and KB Kookmin Bank reported data breaches.

South Korean police, who have launched a probe, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said on Tuesday that signs had emerged that AI was used in some of the hacking incidents and called for heightened cybersecurity measures.

(Reporting by Kyu-seok Shim; Editing by Chris Reese and Ed Davies)

Trump rallies for Paxton in third Texas trip in a month as Republicans defend stronghold

Reuters

08 October, 2026 05:30 am IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

(c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2026

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

By Nandita Bose SAN ANTONIO, Texas, Oct 7 (Reuters) – US President Donald Trump made his third trip to Texas in a month on Wednesday to campaign for Republicans who now face unexpectedly tight midterm election battles as they seek to retain control of Congress.

Trump spoke in a packed arena in San Antonio to support Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton, who is locked in a close race with Democrat James Talarico. A loss on November 3 would complicate the party’s path to retaining its slim Senate majority and mark a major setback in a Republican stronghold.

Trump expressed appreciation for Paxton’s loyalty. He endorsed Paxton in the primary after faulting the incumbent Republican senator, John Cornyn, for not supporting him during tough times.

Show Full Article

“He was with us all the way,” Trump said of Paxton. “He’s a fantastic man and what a job he’s done.”

Supporters, some waving cowboy hats, cheered for Trump and shouted “USA,” drowning out several protesters who interrupted the event in a Texas city led by a Democrat. Trump said the protesters should “get the hell out of here.”

The rally was Trump’s latest effort to mobilize his supporters for Paxton after staging an unusual midterm conventionin Dallas, in part to boost him. But Trump has also publicly criticized his longtime ally, calling Paxton “a pain in the ass sometimes” last week before adding that Republicans “need Ken so badly.”

Trump’s repeated trips to Texas are part of a broader push in Republican-leaning states, which were expected to be safely in hand but have instead become midterm battlegrounds. His 32-day campaign blitz has taken him through Texas, Oklahoma, Alabama, Ohio and Nebraska, while Vice President JD Vance has campaigned in Alaska. Trump and Vance carried all six states in the 2024 presidential election.

Republicans are struggling as voters focus on high costs and the war with Iran, giving Trump record-low approval ratings. A Reuters/Ipsos poll completed Monday put his approval at 32%, with Democrats leading Republicans 44% to 37% among registered voters.

Trump surprised some Republicans in May by backing Paxton in a party runoff over Cornyn, whom party leaders saw as a safer bet. Republicans are now spending heavily to defend territory they once expected to win comfortably.

Trump won the state by 14 points in 2024, but recent polls have shown Talarico ahead of Paxton. Republicans are also defending competitive House of Representatives seats in South Texas. Both Trump and Paxton attacked Talarico repeatedly in their remarks.

For Trump, the stakes are also personal. James Henson, director of the Texas Politics Project at the University of Texas at Austin, said losing the Senate race would be “devastating for Republicans and devastating for Donald Trump” given his support for Paxton. “I think the president clearly will do a lot to try to avoid that outcome,” Henson said.

Trump’s political operation has also poured millions into competitive House races. In San Antonio, Republican Carlos De La Cruz, an Air Force veteran, is running in a newly redrawn district, part of a Republican-led remapping that Democrats have called a partisan gerrymander. De La Cruz is expected to speak at Wednesday’s rally.

AN UNEASY ALLIANCE

Trump and Paxton’s relationship has appeared awkward at times. Paxton was recorded telling donors that Republican candidates’ numbers fell after the Trump-centered convention in Dallas, according to the New York Times, while Trump has publicly mocked Paxton’s clothes, speaking style and appearance.

“So to be honest with you, the numbers, when we did that convention, it dropped our numbers. Everybody’s numbers dropped,” Paxton said in the recording. His campaign has disputed suggestions that the remarks amounted to criticism of Trump. A spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment.

A New York Time/Siena University poll released October 3 showed Talarico leading Paxton 51% to 45% among likely voters. Brandon Rottinghaus, a political science professor at the University of Houston, said rallying Trump’s base was “necessary but not sufficient” for Paxton.

“Trump’s visits are a catch-22,” Rottinghaus said. “The president can inspire as much as he can repel.”

Texas Republican Governor Greg Abbott, a close Trump ally who is also in a closer-than-expected re-election race, planned to skip Wednesday’s rally, citing other campaign events.

“My rallies are saving the Republican Party, again,” Trump said in an all-caps post on Truth Social on Tuesday.

Republicans are betting Trump can still turn out the voters who powered his 2024 victory even as his broader standing has weakened.

The latest Reuters/Ipsos poll showed that just 24% of Hispanic voters approved of his performance. They were an important part of Trump’s success in 2024, when he won nearly half the Hispanic vote, and are a bigger demographic in Texas than most states.

(Reporting by Nandita Bose; Additional reporting by Nolan McCaskill, Bo Erickson and Steve Holland in Washington; Editing by Trevor Hunnicutt, Cynthia Osterman and Deepa Babington)
